title: The Dumbest Military Blunders in History
description:
A warship that sank less than a mile from the dock, a secret telegram that backfired, a wall the enemy simply drove around, a cavalry charge down the wrong valley, and 34,000 soldiers invading an island with nobody on it: these are seven of the dumbest military blunders in history, counted down from seven to one. Every story is real, and we laugh at the mistakes, never at the people who paid for them. Chapters are added automatically.

#history #militaryhistory #funnyhistory #napoleon #historypros

beats.say: In August 1943, about thirty-four thousand American and Canadian soldiers stormed a freezing island near Alaska called Kiska.
Japan had held this island for more than a year, so everyone expected a brutal fight.
They crept through thick fog, rifles ready, hearts pounding.
Anybody see them?
Nope. Not a soul.
That's because the Japanese had already left, more than two weeks earlier.
There was nobody to fight. And somehow, the invasion still went badly wrong.
Today we're counting down seven of the dumbest military blunders in history. That empty island is number one.

show.text: The Dumbest Military Blunders in History
show.sub: Seven blunders. All real. Some very expensive.

show.title: The Ship That Sank Right Away

beats.say: Number seven: the Vasa, a Swedish warship that barely made it out of the harbor.
In the 1620s, Sweden was fighting wars around the Baltic Sea, and it needed a mighty navy.
So King Gustavus Adolphus ordered a showpiece: sixty-four bronze cannons on two gun decks, covered in hundreds of carved statues.
It looked incredible. The problem was simple: too much weight up high, and not enough width down low.
Before launch, Captain Söfring Hansson ran a test: thirty sailors ran from one side of the deck to the other.
After three runs, the ship was rocking so hard that Admiral Klas Fleming stopped the test.
Stop! Stop running, or she'll tip over right here!
So... we launch it anyway?
They launched it anyway.
On August 10, 1628, crowds lined the harbor in Stockholm, Sweden's capital, to watch her sail.
A light gust of wind tipped her over. Water poured in through the open gun holes, and down she went.
She had sailed about thirteen hundred meters. That's less than a mile.
About thirty people drowned. The captain was arrested, but in the end, nobody was punished.
The good news? Cold, low-salt water kept wood-eating worms away, and in 1961 Sweden raised the ship almost whole. Today she's a museum about what not to do.
Number six: the worst secret message ever sent.
In 1917, Germany was fighting Britain and France in World War One, and didn't want America joining in.
So Germany's foreign minister, Arthur Zimmermann, came up with a plan.
If Mexico attacks America, the Americans will be too busy to fight us. Brilliant!
He sent a secret telegram, a message sent by wire, to Germany's ambassador in Mexico. The offer: join Germany against America, and win back Texas, New Mexico and Arizona.
Tiny problem. In London, British codebreakers in a secret office called Room 40 were reading German messages.
They cracked the telegram and handed it to the Americans.
It hit American newspapers in March, and plenty of people said it must be a British fake.
Germany could have just stayed quiet. Instead, Zimmermann told an American reporter this.
I cannot deny it. It is true.

show.text: I cannot deny it. It is true.

beats.say: Mexico's president, Venustiano Carranza, looked at the plan and said no thanks.
And in April 1917, President Woodrow Wilson asked Congress for war. The United States joined the fight against Germany.
It wasn't the only reason, but Zimmermann tried to keep America out, and helped pull it in.
Number five: the wall that got walked around.
After the horrors of World War One, France was determined never to be invaded by Germany again.
So in the 1930s it built the Maginot Line, a chain of huge concrete forts along the border with Germany.
The forts had thick walls, big guns, and even little underground trains.
But the line was weak near the Ardennes, a hilly forest mostly in Belgium and Luxembourg, next to France.
French generals thought tanks couldn't get through those woods quickly. In 1934, Marshal Philippe Pétain, France's World War One hero, called them impenetrable, with the right defenses.
Thus, this sector is not dangerous.
Not dangerous at all, Marshal. No need to worry.
In May 1940, Germany sent a huge force of tanks straight through the Ardennes.
They crawled along narrow forest roads, reached the French town of Sedan in just a few days, and smashed through.
The mighty forts barely mattered. The Germans had simply gone around them.
About six weeks after the attack began, France agreed to stop fighting.
The lesson? A wall only works if the enemy agrees to walk into it.

show.title: The Order That Pointed the Wrong Way

beats.say: Number four: the charge of the Light Brigade.
In 1854, Britain and France were fighting Russia in the Crimean War, on a peninsula in the Black Sea.
The British commander, Lord Raglan, was watching the battle from a hilltop.
He spotted Russians hauling away some captured cannons, and sent a messenger, Captain Louis Nolan, with an order: stop them.
Tell Lord Lucan: stop them taking those guns. Immediately!
Down in the valley, the cavalry commander, Lord Lucan, couldn't see those cannons at all.
Attack what? Which guns?
There, my lord, is your enemy! There are your guns!
Nolan swept his arm toward the big Russian cannons at the far end of a long valley. The wrong ones.
Lucan passed the order to his brother-in-law, Lord Cardigan. The two men hated each other, so they barely talked it over.
Cardigan led about six hundred seventy riders straight down the valley, with Russian guns firing from three sides.
In about twenty minutes, around one hundred ten men were killed, and many more were wounded or captured.
A French general, Pierre Bosquet, watched from the hills and summed it up.
It is magnificent, but it is not war.

show.text: It is magnificent, but it is not war.

beats.say: The riders were incredibly brave. The order was just incredibly bad. The poet Alfred Tennyson made their bravery famous.

show.title: The General Who Ignored a Warning

beats.say: Number three: the Roman general who got a clear warning, and said no thanks.
In 9 AD, Rome was trying to take over Germania, the land of the Germanic tribes, roughly where Germany is today.
The Roman governor there, Publius Quinctilius Varus, had three legions. A legion was a Roman army unit of about five thousand soldiers.
His trusted friend was Arminius, a Germanic prince who had served in the Roman army and even become a Roman citizen.
But secretly, Arminius was uniting the tribes to destroy him.
Then another Germanic chief, Segestes, came to Varus with a warning.
Arminius is plotting against you. Arrest him. Arrest me too, if you don't believe me!
Nonsense. Arminius is my friend.
Soon after, Arminius reported a small revolt, and Varus marched off to crush it. Straight into a trap.
On a narrow strip between forest hills and swamp, in pouring rain, the tribes attacked from the trees for several days.
Almost the whole Roman army was lost, and Varus took his own life.
Back in Rome, Emperor Augustus was devastated. The writer Suetonius says he banged his head against a door, crying out:
Quinctilius Varus, give me back my legions!

show.text: Quinctilius Varus, give me back my legions!

beats.say: Rome never used those three legion numbers again, and never conquered most of Germania. One ignored warning helped keep Rome's border on the Rhine.
Number two: Napoleon picks a fight with Russia.
Napoleon Bonaparte, emperor of France, had beaten almost every army in Europe.
But Russia's ruler, Tsar Alexander the First, had stopped obeying Napoleon's ban on trading with Britain.
Fine. Then I'll just invade Russia.
Be my guest. Russia is very, very big.
In June 1812, he invaded with one of the largest armies Europe had ever seen.
They marched hundreds of miles east, toward Moscow.
The Russians kept retreating, burning crops and villages so the French couldn't find food.
In September, Napoleon finally marched into Moscow. It was almost empty, and within a day, it was on fire.
He waited in the ruins for over a month, expecting the tsar to ask for peace. The tsar refused to talk.
Any letter from the tsar yet?
No, sire. Still nothing.
In October, with little food and winter coming, Napoleon ordered a retreat.
Hunger, disease, freezing cold and constant Russian attacks wore the army down on the long march home.
Estimates vary, but hundreds of thousands never came back.
Napoleon's power never recovered. Less than two years later, he'd lost his throne.

show.title: The Invasion of an Empty Island

beats.say: And number one: back to Kiska, the invasion of an empty island.
In 1942, Japan captured Kiska and Attu, two tiny islands in Alaska's Aleutian chain.
In May 1943, American troops took back Attu in a bloody battle, so everyone knew Kiska was next.
In July, American battleships were guarding the waters near the island. Then one night, their radar, which spots faraway ships using radio waves, showed enemy ships.
Contacts on radar! Lots of them!
Open fire!
The ships fired five hundred eighteen giant shells into the fog. They hit nothing.
There were no enemy ships. The radar was probably picking up echoes from faraway mountains.
Then the fleet left to refuel. And under cover of thick fog, Japanese ships slipped into the harbor and took more than five thousand men off the island in about an hour.
For two more weeks, Allied planes kept bombing the empty island.
Then came the big landing. In the fog, nervous soldiers mistook each other for the enemy. Friendly fire and booby traps killed twenty-eight Americans and four Canadians.
Days later, the American destroyer Abner Read hit a Japanese mine, and seventy-one sailors were killed.
In all, the Allies suffered more than three hundred casualties on an island with no enemy on it.

show.label: Operation Cottage, Kiska
show.sub: Allied casualties. Enemy soldiers found: zero.

beats.say: It's a reminder that in war, fog, fear and bad information can do as much damage as the enemy.
That's the list: a sinking ship, a boomerang telegram, a wall people walked around, a wrong order, an ignored warning, a winter march, and an empty island.
Which one was the dumbest? Tell us in the comments.
